source_text: Esse autem sacrilegium, pudendum aliquid quod Deus fecisse credatur, praeter hanc carnis concupiscentiam iudicare; Christum vero non habuisse hanc concupiscentiam carnis, quae mortalibus facit causam pudoris. Quid igitur ad haec occurreret, non vidisti, videlicet nudum eum, id est Christum, convencticulis debuisse misceri; nec aliquem verecundiae habere respectum, ne sacrilegium quod commentaris incurreret, in carne videlicet sua, quae concupiscentiam non habebat, de suis et Patris operibus erubescens. Si autem ei et concupiscentia non fuit, et tamen ille est pudoris functus officio; irrefutabiliter etiam secundum te approbatur, verecundiam corpori humano debitam, non calori.
pass_a_gloss: But that it is sacrilege to judge something shameful which God is believed to have made, besides this desire of the flesh; but that Christ did not have this desire of the flesh which makes a cause of modesty for mortals. What therefore would meet these things you did not see, namely that he, that is Christ, ought to have mixed naked in assemblies; nor to have any regard of reverence, lest he incur the sacrilege which you invent, blushing namely in his own flesh, which did not have desire, about his own and the Father's works. But if both desire was not in him, and nevertheless he performed the office of modesty; it is irrefutably approved even according to you that reverence is owed to the human body, not to heat.

lemmas.lexica: LS concupiscentia=eager desire; Blaise Christian usage often sexual desire vs nuptiae
LS opus; Blaise God's works vs devil's

pass_b_english: You also said that it is sacrilege to judge anything believed to have been made by God shameful, apart from this desire of the flesh; and that Christ did not have this desire of the flesh, which gives mortals a reason for modesty. Did you not see what follows? Christ should have joined gatherings naked, without any regard for modesty, so as not to incur the sacrilege you invent by being ashamed, in his flesh that had no desire, of his own and his Father’s works. But if he had no such desire and nevertheless observed modesty, then even on your account it is irrefutably proved that modesty is due to the human body, not to its sexual heat.

choices.why: Julian distinguishes nuptiae from concupiscentia; do not flatten to 'lust' as a nature-sin substance.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
Keep Julian's good-of-nature vs good-of-will contrast; do not baptize as 'grace'.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
